finding.claim: reset_password_loose uses loose == to compare the stored reset token with the caller-supplied token, so numeric-looking tokens can be bypassed (e.g. token '0' matches a stored '0e...' string under PHP 8 numeric comparison), enabling password reset without the real token.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (reset.php:2); callers not in repo, treated as attacker-controlled
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw (reset.php:5-6), gated by the comparison at reset.php:4

trace.note: stored token loaded for $email via quoted SELECT
loose == comparison; numeric strings compare as numbers
password hash written for $email on match

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote($email) (SQL-safe, not a token check); $row null guard only; no strict compare, no hash_equals, no type check. Sibling reset_password at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals and is not affected. Exploitability depends on token generation, not in repo: conditional.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset_password_loose. The only check is the $row null guard at reset.php:4, which does not validate the token. $db->quote($email) at reset.php:3 prevents SQL injection but is not a token check. The sibling reset_password at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals, but it is a separate function and does not guard this one.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:4 uses loose `==` between the stored token and the caller's $token, and reset.php:5-6 writes the password hash on match, with no effective control in between. Exploitation still depends on facts outside the repo: whether any caller reaches reset_password_loose with attacker-controlled input (the callers are not in the repo), and whether stored reset tokens can be numeric strings of the `0e...` form. Those cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed or expired: after a successful reset neither function deletes or marks the resets row, and no expiry is checked, so a captured token can be replayed to change the password again.
finding.source: $token and $email parameters (reset.php:2, :12); token previously issued and observed by attacker (email leak, log, referrer)
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw (reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16)

trace.note: SELECT token by email only; no expiry column or created_at check
returns true without deleting or invalidating the resets row
same pattern in reset_password: SELECT with no expiry
returns true without consuming the token

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Whether the caller deletes the token or enforces expiry is UNCERTAIN because the caller is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset.php. The only other file in the directory is reset.php itself, so no caller, token-deletion, or expiry logic is present. reset.php:3 and :13 select the token by email alone, with no expiry column or created_at check.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (reset.php:3 SELECT by email only, :5-7 and :15-17 update the password and return true without touching the resets row), but whether a replayed token is actually accepted depends on a caller outside this repo that may delete or expire the row, and the attacker also needs a previously leaked token, so this cannot be settled from the code available.
